**General Certificate of Education Board - General Certificate of Education Examination. English Language 3 (0730), ADVANCED LEVEL, June 2025. Paper 3: Section A - Summary Writing; Section B - Text Reconstruction; Section C - Editing. Duration: two and a quarter hours.**

ALL THE QUESTIONS ARE COMPULSORY. THEY CARRY EQUAL MARKS.

Read all instructions on BOTH the question paper and the answer booklet very carefully. Failure to obey these instructions or to number your work as on the question paper will cause you to lose marks.

Any unusual mark, sign or unnecessary disclosure of your identity will be considered as an attempt to cheat and will earn you a penalty.

In the SUMMARY WRITING question, use mainly your own words. Indiscriminate copying of portions of the passage as your answer will earn you no marks.

You are reminded of the necessity for good English and orderly presentation in your answers.

Texte à trous : le sujet imprime des blancs numérotés (1) à (15). Plusieurs réponses sont possibles pour certains blancs ; le corrigé donne une réponse modèle et les variantes dans la colonne Rule. Pour le blanc (4), la question négative « Aren't you married? » est rapportée par « he isn't » (« if he isn't married »), forme jugée la plus fidèle ; « he is not » est équivalent.
Le blanc (2) précède le mot imprimé « laundry » : la réponse modèle est « he does his », mais « he does » est aussi correct. Un point par blanc est une hypothèse de correction, pas un barème imprimé.
Le sujet imprime « I'II » (avec deux I majuscules, lecture d'un « I'll ») dans « I'II not hesitate » : recopié « I'll » ; « I've the impression » est recopié tel quel.

**SECTION B: TEXT RECONSTRUCTION (15 MARKS)**

**Read the following conversation between Sam and Tom carefully. Then without altering the numbering, copy and complete the reconstructed form by filling the blanks with the correct word/expression.**

**Sam:** Do you sell in the market on Sundays?

**Tom:** I go to church every Sunday morning. Then in the afternoon, I do my laundry since I don't have time to do so during the week.

**Sam:** Aren't you married? Living a bachelor's life isn't good for a young successful businessman like you.

**Tom:** I will get married at the right time. Once I see a beautiful and well behaved girl, I'll not hesitate to take her to the altar.

**Sam:** That's a good decision. I believe you will be more responsible if you eventually take a wife. I assure you of my total support when the time comes.

**Tom:** I know that you will never disappoint me. We've been friends for a very long time now.

**Sam:** Certainly and that's why I always defend you when you are criticised. I've the impression that our friendship will grow from strength to strength.

questions.corrige_markdown:
**Reconstructed form** (the conversation is turned into reported speech: pronouns and possessives change person, verbs keep the present tense because the reporting verbs "asks", "replies", "adds" are in the present)

Sam asks Tom if he sells in the market on Sundays. Tom replies that **he goes** to church every Sunday morning. Then in the afternoon, **he does his** laundry since **he doesn't** have time to do so within the week. Sam asks Tom if **he isn't** married. He adds that living a bachelor's life **isn't** good for a young successful businessman like **him**. Tom replies that he will get married at the right time. Once **he sees** a beautiful and well behaved girl, **he will** not hesitate to take her to the altar. Sam applauds Tom's decision and adds that **he believes** Tom will be more responsible if he eventually **takes** a wife. He **assures** Tom of his total support when the time comes. Tom **knows** that Sam will never disappoint him. **They have** been friends for a very long time now. Sam agrees with him and says that is why he always **defends** Tom when **he is** criticised. He has the impression that their friendship will grow from strength to strength.

**Before / after / rule**

| Blank | Answer | Rule |
|---|---|---|
| (1) | he goes | Direct speech "I go" becomes "he goes": third person singular, present simple. The reporting verb "replies" is in the present, so there is no back-shift of tense. The blank needs the subject and the verb together. |
| (2) | he does his | "I do my laundry" becomes "he does his laundry": pronoun and possessive change from first to third person; "do" takes -es. Also accepted: "he does" ("he does laundry"). |
| (3) | he doesn't | "I don't have time" becomes "he doesn't have time": third person singular auxiliary "doesn't" before the base verb "have". Also: "he does not". |
| (4) | he isn't | "Aren't you married?" is a yes/no question, so it is reported with "if" and statement order: "if he isn't married". Also: "he is not". |
| (5) | isn't | "Living a bachelor's life isn't good" keeps the present tense after "adds that" (present reporting verb): "isn't" or "is not". The verb must agree with the singular gerund subject "living". |
| (6) | him | "like you" becomes "like him": the second person pronoun "you" is replaced by the third person object pronoun after the preposition "like". |
| (7) | he sees | "Once I see" becomes "Once he sees": present simple after "once" (a time clause never takes "will"), third person singular -s. |
| (8) | he will | "I'll not hesitate" becomes "he will not hesitate": the blank is followed by "not", so the answer is "he will" (the printed "will get married" shows that the tense is kept). |
| (9) | he believes | "I believe you will be more responsible" becomes "he believes Tom will be more responsible": the reporting phrase "adds that" needs a subject and verb in the present, third person singular. Also: "he thinks", "he feels". |
| (10) | takes | "if you eventually take a wife" becomes "if he eventually takes a wife": present simple after "if", third person singular -s. The word "eventually" is printed just before the blank. |
| (11) | assures | "I assure you of my total support" becomes "He assures Tom of his total support": the same verb in the third person singular (assure someone of something). Also: "promises", "pledges". |
| (12) | knows | "I know that you will never disappoint me" becomes "Tom knows that Sam will never disappoint him": third person singular, present simple, followed by a that-clause. Also: "believes", "is sure". |
| (13) | They have | "We've been friends" becomes "They have been friends": the pronoun "we" becomes "they" because the narrator speaks about Sam and Tom. The printed "been" requires the present perfect auxiliary "have". |
| (14) | defends | "I always defend you" becomes "he always defends Tom": third person singular -s on the verb after the adverb "always" (the adverb is printed before the blank). |
| (15) | he is | "when you are criticised" becomes "when he is criticised": "you" (Tom, the person addressed) becomes "he"; the passive "is criticised" is completed by the printed participle. |

**Marking grid (15 marks).** There are 15 blanks for 15 marks, so each correct blank is worth one mark (the scheme itself is not printed). A word or expression earns the mark when the person, the tense and the agreement are right and the spelling is correct; the numbering must not be altered.

**Common mistakes**

1. Keeping the pronouns of the direct speech ("I", "you", "my") instead of changing them to the third person: "Tom replies that I go to church".
2. Back-shifting the tense when the reporting verb is in the present ("he went", "he would get married"): the printed text "he will get married" shows that the tense stays.
3. Forgetting third person -s or the auxiliary "does/doesn't" ("he don't", "he sees" written "he see"), or writing a blank answer that does not fit the words printed after it ("they been" instead of "They have").
